initial_relationship: Doctor and former patient
how_they_meet: Bhaskar had earlier treated Renu for pneumonia.
courtship_pattern: Bhaskar keeps his feelings to himself; Anand discovers them, helps him express his love and persuades Renu's mother to bless the marriage.
emotional_dynamic: Reticent attachment on Bhaskar's side, drawn out by his friend; Renu's own feelings are not described in the sources.
pair_conflict: None documented; the obstacle is Bhaskar's reserve.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between the two is documented, only Bhaskar's hesitation to speak.
external_opposition_explanation: Renu's mother has to be persuaded to bless the marriage, which Anand does.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is incidental. Bhaskar's story is his friendship with Anand and his despair as a doctor who cannot cure poverty and disease.
actor_transformation: Anand's intervention moves the withdrawn, pessimistic Bhaskar to declare his love.
relationship_outcome: Renu's mother blesses the marriage; the fetched plot summary does not show a wedding.
relationship_analysis: A subplot that serves Anand's characterisation: the dying man arranges happiness for his friend. The romance is courteous and brokered by others, and Renu's own voice is largely absent from the sources.
critical_reading: The Hindu (2021) praises Bachchan's subtle performance as a counterpoint to Khanna but does not comment on the romance.

initial_relationship: Strangers, then a prospective arranged match
how_they_meet: The day before the arranged viewing, Ram's taxi breaks down and Kusum, not knowing who he is, gives him a lift; when her own car breaks down she tells him about Banke's rumours.
who_initiates: The families arrange the match; Kusum greets Ram openly at the viewing
courtship_pattern: A chance meeting followed by an arranged viewing at which Kusum introduces herself joyfully and Ram accepts her, already aware of the gossip.
emotional_dynamic: Ram's steady acceptance against Kusum's open, naive exuberance.
pair_conflict: None between them in the sources. The obstacle is Ravi's refusal to approve the match, which Ram has promised to honour.
pair_friction_explanation: Ram dismisses the gossip and accepts Kusum at once; no conflict between the pair is documented.
external_opposition_explanation: Banke's rumours have ruined Kusum's reputation and driven off suitors. Ravi, whose approval Ram has promised to seek and who is Kusum's estranged brother, withholds it.
lover_boy_explanation: Ram is defined as much by loyalty to Ravi and his promise as by romance; he accepts Kusum readily, but the sources show little courtship.
relationship_analysis: The film sets a man's personal loyalty against a woman's damaged reputation. Ram already knows and dismisses the rumours, so the drama comes from his promise to Ravi rather than from any doubt about Kusum. Kusum's indifference to gossip is framed as naivety, and both reviewers found the innocence overplayed.
critical_reading: MemsaabStory (2008) found the film dull, with Tanuja its only spark and Bachchan showing only flashes of charisma. Brown Car Guy (2017) thought the role, first meant for Jeetendra, did him no favours.

initial_relationship: Acquaintances; Kumar already loves Asha when the story begins
courtship_pattern: Kumar cannot express his love. After Asha falls for Rajeshwar he demands her hand from her uncle, kills the uncle when refused and frames Rajeshwar for the murder.
emotional_dynamic: One-sided infatuation. Asha does not return Kumar's love and stays loyal to Rajeshwar.
pair_conflict: Asha loves Rajeshwar; Kumar's crime is meant to remove her guardian and her lover.
pair_friction_explanation: Asha rejects Kumar's love and later bargains with him to save the man he framed. The hostility is mostly hidden, but the two want opposite things.
external_opposition_explanation: Asha's love for Rajeshwar and her uncle's refusal of Kumar's proposal.
lover_boy_explanation: Love is Kumar's motive, but the role is a scheming murderer rather than a romantic hero; the main Wikipedia article calls him an infatuated lover-turned-murderer.
actor_transformation: Asha's offer to stay with him if he saves Rajeshwar makes Kumar accept that she will always love Rajeshwar; he writes a full confession and kills himself.
relationship_outcome: No union. Kumar confesses to the murder, clears Rajeshwar and commits suicide.
relationship_analysis: The film presents Kumar's love as a destructive infatuation. His confession gives him a measure of redemption, but the relationship is one-sided throughout, and Asha's promise to stay with him is a bargain made under duress to save the man she loves.
critical_reading: The Hindu calls the plot the sinister machination of a man who cannot accept that the woman he loves has chosen another, and says Bachchan shone in a negative role that risked typecasting him.

initial_relationship: Lovers
courtship_pattern: Mohan falls in love with Asha and they marry in a temple.
emotional_dynamic: A love marriage broken off early. When they meet again ten years later, the bond is buried under Mohan's new family and a reversed hierarchy in which Asha is his superior.
pair_conflict: Their hidden marriage, which office rumour and Seema's suspicion bring to the surface.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is described. Tension comes from the buried past and the reversal at work; The Hindu says Mohan left Asha to fend for herself.
external_opposition_explanation: Mohan's mother refuses to accept the marriage and the couple is separated; his parents tell him Asha has died; later his second marriage and office gossip stand between them.
lover_boy_explanation: Mohan's romantic identity is limited to the early love marriage; he is mainly a clerk and family man caught between two wives.
female_transformation: From an abandoned, pregnant wife to a District Collector who gives her life to save her husband's second wife.
relationship_outcome: Asha dies saving Seema and her eyes are given to Seema; Mohan remains with Seema and the children, including Asha's child.
relationship_analysis: The film resolves a bigamy problem through the first wife's death and sacrifice, so Mohan keeps his second family without having to choose. Asha's professional rise sits uneasily beside a plot that rewards her self-effacement.
critical_reading: The Hindu found Mala Sinha the film's only notable performance, with little scope for Bachchan, and called the climax contrived. A contemporary Film World review called the screenplay old-fashioned, trite and incoherent.

initial_relationship: Married (Mohan's second marriage)
courtship_pattern: Mohan marries Seema in South India after his parents tell him Asha has died.
emotional_dynamic: A settled, happy marriage with two children, shaken by rumours of an affair between Mohan and his new boss.
pair_conflict: Seema's suspicion of Mohan and Asha, and her discovery of their earlier marriage.
pair_friction_explanation: The rumours disturb Seema, who looks into Mohan's past and extracts the truth from Asha. The conflict is serious but comes from a hidden past rather than open hostility.
external_opposition_explanation: Office gossip started by Mansukh, and Mohan's undisclosed first marriage, threaten the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Mohan is a husband and father here; no courtship is described.
female_transformation: Loses her sight in the accident in which Asha dies and sees again through Asha's eyes.
relationship_outcome: The marriage survives; Mohan, Seema, both fathers and the three children pay homage to Asha.
relationship_analysis: The second marriage is the one the film preserves. Mohan's silence about his first marriage causes the crisis, yet the cost falls on the two women: one dies, the other is blinded.
critical_reading: The Hindu calls the climax that reunites Mohan and Seema contrived.

initial_relationship: Admirer and the woman he protects
how_they_meet: Ravi, described as Mala's admirer and bodyguard, joins her on the Bombay–Goa bus after Sharma puts an armed henchman aboard to kill her.
courtship_pattern: Protection on the road: Ravi guards Mala throughout the journey and she comes to trust and then love him.
emotional_dynamic: Protective hero and endangered runaway; trust turns into love.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Sharma, whose murder of Verma Mala witnessed, sends an armed henchman after her.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi is mainly a protector in a comic road film; the romance grows out of that role.
relationship_analysis: The romance grows out of protection during a comic road journey. The cast list names Ravi's father as Ramlal, whose son Mala's parents chose for her, so the runaway appears to fall for the match she rejected; the fetched plot summary does not say how the film treats this.
critical_reading: No review of the pairing was found. The main Wikipedia article notes that Salim–Javed chose Bachchan for Zanjeer after seeing him chew gum through a fight in this film.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she admires his poetry without knowing him
how_they_meet: Akash overhears one of his poems being sung at a courtesan's house, goes in and meets the singer, Shabnam.
courtship_pattern: Acquaintance through his poetry turns into mutual love; Akash leaves his father's house to continue the relationship.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual devotion between a poet and a courtesan who already admires his work.
pair_conflict: None documented between them; the conflict is social.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Amina Bai and Akash's father both oppose the match; Amina Bai sells Shabnam to a Nawab; after Amina Bai's death Shabnam is tried for murder with Akash's father as prosecutor.
lover_boy_explanation: Akash is a romantic poet whose defining choice is to leave his father's house for Shabnam.
relationship_analysis: A courtesan romance in which the hero's poetry bridges the class divide. The father–son conflict becomes literal when the father prosecutes the woman his son loves, and the Wikipedia summary says the film examines the morals people impose on others but not on themselves.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing; the film article notes that Bachchan and Bhaduri fell in love during the shoot.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Bansi, escaping the Bombay ashram to which she was sold, meets Birju, who hides her from her pursuers.
who_initiates: Birju offers protection; who declares love first is not documented
courtship_pattern: Protection develops into a close bond and then love.
emotional_dynamic: A protective, supportive man and a vulnerable woman on the run.
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the pair is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Bansi's pursuers from the ashram, and continuing threats and social obstacles.
lover_boy_explanation: Birju is the title romantic hero whose role is to protect and stand by Bansi; the sources give no detail beyond that.
relationship_analysis: The only fetched plot is a short Wikipedia summary with no ending, so the pairing can be described only in outline: a rescue romance in which the woman's past exploitation creates the social obstacle and the man's steady support is the romantic ideal.
critical_reading: No review was found.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Jai sees Neeta being thrown onto the street by her aunt and uncle, finds her a place to stay and gets her an audition at his agency.
courtship_pattern: Jai helps Neeta and falls in love with her as they work together; Neeta instead falls for their married boss Choudhary, who secretly gives her an engagement ring and borrows Jai's flat.
emotional_dynamic: Jai's quiet devotion against Neeta's trusting attraction to a man who hides his marriage.
pair_conflict: Neeta's attachment to Choudhary.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is described; the tension is Neeta's preference for Choudhary over Jai.
external_opposition_explanation: Choudhary, Jai's employer, courts Neeta while concealing his marriage and controls Jai's promotion.
lover_boy_explanation: Jai's choice between career and love is the centre of his story, handled with humour; he is a romantic lead but also a compromised careerist.
relationship_analysis: Jai's career depends on lending his flat to the boss who is seducing the woman he loves, so the romance tests whether he will put love before his job. The fetched review withholds the answer.
critical_reading: MemsaabStory (2009) says Jai's dilemma is handled with humour and sensitivity before the last half-hour turns grim and over the top; a reader comment finds Neeta's character gullible.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she believes he is the writer Deepak
how_they_meet: Hiding from the police in a theatre, Shyamu is caught leaving Mala's make-up room and claims to be Deepak, the writer the theatre is expecting.
who_initiates: Shyamu declares his love and Mala returns it
courtship_pattern: Mala's honesty inspires Shyamu to reform. After assuming Deepak's identity he declares his love to her portrait; she overhears and welcomes it.
emotional_dynamic: A warm, principled woman and a reformed thief living under a false identity.
pair_conflict: Shyamu's imposture, and Mala's belief that he is a womaniser when he plays along with Rajni to recover Deepak's letters.
pair_friction_explanation: Mala suspects Shyamu of betraying her with Rajni and later learns his real identity from Inspector Kumar; the rift rests on his deception.
external_opposition_explanation: Inspector Kumar's pursuit, and Rajni, who expects Deepak's romantic attention after their correspondence.
lover_boy_explanation: Love for Mala drives Shyamu's reform, but the film is a thief's redemption drama and the reviewer found Bachchan aloof in the romantic scenes.
chemistry_explanation: The Old is Gold reviewer found Mumtaz warm and sparkly and Bachchan aloof and clearly uncomfortable in their romantic scenes, calling them an odd pair.
actor_transformation: Mala's view that a good person stays good in hard times prompts Shyamu to give up theft.
relationship_analysis: The romance is the moral engine of a reform plot: the heroine's honesty turns the thief, but the relationship rests on a false identity, and his pretend courtship of Rajni makes the deception visible to her.
critical_reading: The Old is Gold review follows Shyamu into a quagmire of deception; in the comments its author calls the lead pair an odd match.

initial_relationship: Police officer and witness
how_they_meet: Mala, a street performer bribed to keep quiet about a fatal traffic accident, is questioned by Vijay, who takes her to the morgue to see the children's bodies.
courtship_pattern: After she identifies the culprit and flees Teja's men, Vijay shelters her; they find they are both orphans, he places her with his brother and sister-in-law, and Mala falls for him.
emotional_dynamic: Her growing love tempering his solitary rage.
pair_conflict: Mala wants Vijay to give up his revenge; he promises reluctantly.
pair_friction_explanation: Mala begs him to abandon vengeance and he agrees against his nature; she later relents and tells him to do what is right.
external_opposition_explanation: Teja's men hunt Mala after she breaks her silence, and Teja frames Vijay, who is jailed for six months.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay is defined by trauma, anger and justice; romance is a counterweight rather than a motive.
actor_transformation: Mala's plea makes Vijay promise to stop his revenge; the promise gives way after he hears D'Silva's story.
female_transformation: From a bribed street performer to a witness who gives the bribe to an orphanage and learns housekeeping and English under Vijay's sister-in-law.
relationship_outcome: They drive off together with Sher Khan after Vijay kills Teja.
relationship_analysis: Zanjeer broke with the romantic films before it, and its romance reflects that: Mala is the moral voice asking the angry hero to step back, while the film ultimately endorses his violence and she releases him to pursue it. Her domestic training under the sister-in-law presents reform in period terms.
critical_reading: The main Wikipedia article describes Zanjeer as a violent crime film in sharp contrast to the romantic films that preceded it; no fetched review assesses the pair.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Subir, a star singer with no plans to marry, meets Uma, a musically gifted village girl.
courtship_pattern: Subir falls in love with Uma, marries her and brings her to Bombay, where he encourages her to sing with him.
emotional_dynamic: A mentor-husband whose support for his wife's talent turns to rivalry when she eclipses him.
pair_conflict: Subir's pride and jealousy at Uma's greater success.
pair_friction_explanation: Subir's jealousy tears the marriage apart and the couple separates; the rupture comes from inside the relationship.
external_opposition_explanation: The public's preference for Uma triggers the crisis, but the film places the conflict in Subir's ego; his aunt's criticism helps reunite them.
lover_boy_explanation: Subir courts and marries Uma and the film is about their bond, but he is shown mainly as a proud, jealous husband rather than a romantic idealist.
actor_transformation: His aunt's criticism makes Subir recognise his vanity, and he reconciles with Uma.
female_transformation: From a village girl to a singer more successful than her husband, then a grieving wife after a miscarriage.
relationship_outcome: Reconciled; they sing together.
relationship_analysis: Abhimaan studies male ego inside a love marriage: the husband who brings his wife's talent into public view cannot bear its success. The rupture is punished through Uma's miscarriage and repaired through Subir's contrition, so the change is his but the suffering is hers.
critical_reading: The BBC (2023) calls it a marital drama still relevant after 50 years and quotes a viewer who found the envious husband believable because ego often comes between a couple, especially where men are uncomfortable with wives doing better.

initial_relationship: Business associates: she makes the gur he sells
how_they_meet: Majubi, a widow in Moti's village, already prepares the gur that Moti sells.
courtship_pattern: Moti proposes only to avoid paying Majubi's wage; surprised at first, she accepts, unaware of his motive.
emotional_dynamic: Her genuine attachment and labour exploited by his calculation.
pair_conflict: Moti's hidden motive and his divorce of Majubi on a false charge of infidelity with her brother-in-law.
pair_friction_explanation: Moti deceives Majubi into marriage and casts her off with a false accusation; she curses him, and when he returns years later she first meets him with anger.
external_opposition_explanation: Moti's desire for Phool Banu, not outside pressure, ends the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Moti feigns courtship of Majubi for profit; there is no romantic devotion on his side.
female_transformation: From a widow persuaded into remarriage to a woman who confronts Moti, marries the courteous fish trader Nadeer and finally forgives Moti's plea.
relationship_outcome: Divorced; Majubi marries Nadeer. When the ruined Moti asks her to make gur for him she recognises his remorse, and she and Phool Banu embrace.
relationship_analysis: The marriage is a labour arrangement disguised as romance. The film treats Moti's use of Majubi as a moral failing punished by his business collapse, and ThePrint reads it as a critique of how women's domestic and productive labour is taken for granted.
critical_reading: ThePrint says Nutan's Majubi dominates the film, astounding in her range from a vulnerable widow easily talked into remarriage to the woman who confronts Moti.

initial_relationship: Strangers from a neighbouring village
how_they_meet: Moti meets Phool Banu during the off-season and falls in love with her.
courtship_pattern: Moti asks her father for her hand; the father demands a Rs 500 bride price, which Moti raises by exploiting Majubi before marrying Phool Banu.
emotional_dynamic: Moti's infatuation turns to frustration and violence when Phool Banu cannot make gur or run the household as Majubi did.
pair_conflict: Phool Banu's failure at gur-making, Moti's mounting debts and his violence.
pair_friction_explanation: Moti beats Phool Banu with a stick when she lets the gur burn; they reconcile through her father, and she leaves again when he gives up the trade.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father's demand for a bride price that Moti cannot afford.
lover_boy_explanation: Moti is a village charmer who courts Phool Banu and compromises his integrity to marry her, but the film exposes the selfishness in that devotion.
female_transformation: From an innocent bride to a wife who refuses to measure herself by Moti's expectations and finally embraces Majubi.
relationship_outcome: Following Moti to Majubi's house, Phool Banu overhears his plea, and she and Majubi weep and embrace. The fetched sources do not say how Moti and Phool Banu's marriage continues.
relationship_analysis: The 'love of his life' is an ideal Moti bought with another woman's labour; once married, his attachment gives way to resentment and violence. The film resolves the story through the two women rather than the man.
critical_reading: ThePrint says Padma Khanna does her job well as the attractive, innocent Phool Banu, who is not ashamed of lacking Majubi's skills.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Amit, a taxi driver, saves Sapna from the smuggler Heera, who wants her for his pleasure.
courtship_pattern: After rescuing her, Amit promises to marry Sapna once she is acquitted of a false robbery charge.
emotional_dynamic: Rescuer and rescued turning into devoted fiancés; Sapna puts his family's unity before her own happiness.
pair_conflict: None between them; Sapna leaves to avoid dividing Amit's family.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is described; Sapna's decision to leave is self-sacrifice rather than conflict.
external_opposition_explanation: Heera's pursuit of Sapna, the false charge that sends her to prison, and Amit's father's refusal, on the eve of the wedding, to accept a slum-dweller bride.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit rescues Sapna, promises marriage and keeps searching for her after she disappears; romance organises his story.
female_transformation: From a slum dweller fleeing her stepfather to a stage star in Calcutta who turns down another proposal and returns to Amit.
relationship_outcome: Reunited.
relationship_analysis: The pairing follows the self-sacrificing heroine pattern: Sapna removes herself to protect Amit's family, and his search proves his fidelity. Class prejudice is the obstacle; the fetched summary does not show how the father's objection is overcome.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Lovers
how_they_meet: Neela is already Ravi's girlfriend when the story begins; they are due to marry.
courtship_pattern: No courtship is shown; the planned marriage is interrupted by the murder case.
emotional_dynamic: A devoted partner who cannot make sense of Ravi's confession and helps him once he admits his innocence.
pair_conflict: Ravi's false confession, which he does not explain to Neela until he summons her to the hospital.
pair_friction_explanation: The confession strains the relationship, but no quarrel is described; Neela responds with bewilderment and then support.
external_opposition_explanation: A murder charge, a death sentence and a brain tumour threaten to separate the couple for good.
lover_boy_explanation: Ravi's story is organised around his family, his illness and the murder case; Neela matters, but romance is not his driving motive.
female_transformation: From Ravi's fiancée to his ally in escaping and finding the real killer.
relationship_outcome: Ravi is acquitted; the fetched plot does not describe the couple's future.
relationship_analysis: Neela is a loyal partner whose faith survives Ravi's confession, and she takes an active part in his escape and pursuit of the murderer. The obstacles are external: illness, the law and the real killer.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Vijay meets Anita, a prostitute, at a bar.
courtship_pattern: A sexual relationship that deepens into commitment; Anita urges him to remove his tattoo by plastic surgery.
emotional_dynamic: Anita is the one person to whom Vijay explains the wound behind the tattoo; her pregnancy turns him towards marriage and surrender.
pair_conflict: None described; Vijay rejects her suggestion to erase the tattoo.
pair_friction_explanation: The only disagreement is over the tattoo, and it is a confession rather than a quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Samant's men beat Anita to death in revenge just as Vijay decides to leave the underworld, marry her and surrender.
lover_boy_explanation: The relationship gives Vijay a reason to reform, but his mother, his brother and his father's disgrace drive his story.
actor_transformation: Anita's pregnancy makes Vijay decide to give up crime, marry her and surrender, so that their child will not be scarred as he was.
relationship_outcome: Anita is killed; Vijay murders Samant and his men in revenge.
relationship_analysis: The film gives Vijay a relationship outside marriage with a woman he met at a bar and makes her pregnancy his reason to reform. Her murder closes that route and brands him a criminal for good.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Presented to her as her long-lost brother
how_they_meet: Badal enters the Singh household posing as Sunita's kidnapped brother Chimpoo.
courtship_pattern: Not described beyond their falling in love while he is believed to be her brother.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual love conducted under a false sibling identity.
pair_conflict: Badal's imposture; the fetched plots do not say when Sunita learns the truth.
pair_friction_explanation: The deception is Badal's and implicates Sunita, but no quarrel between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Their love must be hidden from a household that believes Badal is the son, especially the ailing Rukmini; Maharaj keeps the secret.
lover_boy_explanation: Falling in love prompts Badal's confession, the turning point of his story, but the fetched plots say little about the courtship.
actor_transformation: Love for Sunita leads Badal to confess his imposture to Maharaj.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: The romance creates the film's central taboo: a couple the household sees as brother and sister. Badal's love turns an impostor into a truth-teller, but the fetched plots stop before showing how the family learns the truth.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she believes he is the married Parimal
how_they_meet: Sukumar, posing as Parimal, meets Vasudha, the younger sister of Prashant's wife Lata.
courtship_pattern: He grows close to her while in disguise; she suspects a married man's infidelity until he reveals the prank.
emotional_dynamic: Suspicion giving way to trust once the deception is confessed.
pair_conflict: Vasudha believes Sukumar is a married man making advances.
pair_friction_explanation: Her disapproval comes from the mistaken identity and ends when he tells her the truth.
external_opposition_explanation: The prank itself, and Lata's fury over the apparent affair; the couple escape from home to marry.
lover_boy_explanation: Sukumar's part in the prank turns into a courtship that ends in elopement; romance is his main thread in the film.
actor_transformation: From a stand-in in a prank to a man who confesses the deception and elopes.
female_transformation: From suspecting him of infidelity to eloping with him.
relationship_outcome: They marry in a temple with Prashant's blessing.
relationship_analysis: The pairing is a comic by-product of Parimal's prank: the disguise that makes Sukumar look like an adulterer also brings the couple together, and honesty resolves it.
critical_reading: Outlook calls the film one of the most entertaining Hindi comedies but does not discuss the pairing.

initial_relationship: Neighbours
how_they_meet: Shekhar moves in as Mili's new neighbour.
courtship_pattern: Mili's cheerfulness gradually draws the depressed, alcoholic Shekhar out of himself, and he falls in love with her without knowing she is ill.
emotional_dynamic: She lifts his despair; he comes to protect her.
pair_conflict: Shekhar's impulse to leave rather than watch Mili die.
pair_friction_explanation: His planned departure is the only rift, and a neighbour's reproach ends it.
external_opposition_explanation: Pernicious anaemia, considered untreatable at the time, threatens to end the relationship with Mili's death.
lover_boy_explanation: Love for Mili transforms Shekhar and drives him to marry her and seek a cure abroad.
actor_transformation: From a rigid, hardened man to someone who embraces life (Indian Express).
relationship_outcome: Married; they fly to Switzerland hoping to find a cure.
relationship_analysis: As in Anand, Bachchan's withdrawn character is changed by a dying optimist, but here the bond becomes romantic and leads to marriage. Illness is the only obstacle, and the open ending leaves the couple's future uncertain.
critical_reading: The Indian Express compares Mili with Anand and says Bachchan's character in both is transformed from a rigid, hardened man; it does not assess the pair's chemistry.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Jai arrives in Ramgarh and meets Radha, Thakur Baldev Singh's widowed, reclusive daughter-in-law.
courtship_pattern: Quiet feeling rather than open courtship; the fetched sources describe no declaration.
emotional_dynamic: Restrained and largely unspoken, set against Radha's grief and seclusion.
pair_conflict: None described.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Radha's widowhood keeps her secluded, and the war with Gabbar Singh ends in Jai's death before their feelings can go anywhere.
lover_boy_explanation: Jai's feelings for Radha deepen his story, but friendship with Veeru and the fight against Gabbar define him.
relationship_outcome: Jai dies; Radha is left devastated.
relationship_analysis: The Jai–Radha thread is a muted counterpoint to Veeru and Basanti's comic romance: feelings that stay unspoken because of Radha's widowhood and are cut off by Jai's death.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Rescuer and the woman he saved
how_they_meet: In the past, Rajesh saved Mala when she was about to kill herself and took her home to his mother and sister.
courtship_pattern: Acquaintance ripened into affection and then love (Conversations Over Chai); the fetched sources do not say why they parted.
emotional_dynamic: Mala's buried feelings collide with her duty to her husband and her fear for her son.
pair_conflict: Rajesh, a fugitive, shuts himself in with Mala's son while her husband hunts him.
pair_friction_explanation: Mala will protect her son at any cost, even against the man she once loved; the conflict is serious but comes from his situation rather than hostility between them.
external_opposition_explanation: Mala is now married to the inspector pursuing Rajesh for murder, and the story ends with Rajesh's death.
lover_boy_explanation: The love story lives in flashback; in the present Rajesh is a fugitive driven by revenge for his sister.
female_transformation: Mala refuses to compromise her own dignity or her husband's self-respect, and answers her husband's accusations cuttingly (Conversations Over Chai).
relationship_outcome: Rajesh dies at the end.
relationship_analysis: The film turns a past romance into a moral trap in which Mala's old love and her present family are set against each other inside her own house. The review credits Mala with more depth than a decorative heroine.
critical_reading: Conversations Over Chai calls Mala a strong character and praises the three leads' performances; it does not rate the pair's chemistry.

initial_relationship: Married
how_they_meet: Already married when the story begins; Radha gives birth to their son Raju.
courtship_pattern: Not applicable
emotional_dynamic: A principled wife who refuses tainted compensation and silently accepts her husband's turn to revenge.
pair_conflict: Dharma's descent into crime, which Radha understands but does not challenge.
pair_friction_explanation: Radha knows Dharma has killed Sujit but keeps quiet; there is moral distance rather than open quarrel.
external_opposition_explanation: Dharma's employers frame and jail him; Radha loses their unborn baby while he is in prison and is later killed by Rajan in an attempt on Dharma's life.
lover_boy_explanation: Dharma is a husband and father; revenge, not romance, drives him.
relationship_outcome: Radha is killed by Rajan in a failed attempt on Dharma.
relationship_analysis: Radha stands for the honest life Dharma loses: she refuses his bosses' money and works herself to exhaustion while he is in jail. Her silence about the killing shows how far his revenge has carried the marriage from its village beginnings.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Acquaintances from London
how_they_meet: Raju, Dharma's son and Bachchan's second role, meets Geeta in London.
courtship_pattern: Not described; Raju returns home wanting to marry her.
emotional_dynamic: Unclear from the fetched plot.
pair_conflict: None described.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Dharma opposes the match because he has promised Raju to his business partner's daughter.
lover_boy_explanation: Raju's wish to marry Geeta sets him against his father, but the fetched plot gives the romance little space.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched plot.
relationship_analysis: A generational echo of the first half: the son's love match collides with the father's business promise. The fetched plot does not resolve it.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Fellow students
how_they_meet: Amit recites his poetry on the college campus in Kashmir, where he meets Pooja.
courtship_pattern: They fall in love as students; before parting, Pooja makes Amit promise to marry and keep writing poetry.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual first love, followed by Amit's lasting bitterness at losing her.
pair_conflict: Amit never forgives or forgets Pooja's marriage.
pair_friction_explanation: Twenty years later Pooja realises Amit has not forgiven her; the tension is resentment rather than open hostility.
external_opposition_explanation: Pooja's parents arrange her marriage to Vijay against her wishes, separating the couple permanently.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit's identity as a poet is bound to his love for Pooja; he gives up poetry when he loses her.
actor_transformation: Heartbreak turns the poet into a hard businessman who stops writing.
female_transformation: From a student in love to a wife and television host who introduces Amit to the public as a famous poet.
relationship_outcome: Parted by her marriage; they become friends again after Vijay learns the truth.
relationship_analysis: Lost love is the source of Amit's bitterness and, later, of his harshness towards his wife; Vijay's acceptance and Pooja's renewed friendship let him put the past behind him. Pooja's agency is limited: she yields to her parents and asks Amit to move on.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Married
how_they_meet: Amit is married to Anjali when the story resumes twenty years later; the fetched plot does not describe the wedding.
courtship_pattern: Not applicable
emotional_dynamic: Anjali fears for her marriage and hides her past; Amit turns punitive when he learns it.
pair_conflict: Anjali's concealment of Pinky, her daughter from a premarital relationship.
pair_friction_explanation: Amit furiously punishes Anjali and Pinky with silence, and Anjali prepares to leave him.
external_opposition_explanation: The stigma attached to Anjali's premarital child and her fear of exposure.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit is a rigid husband here, not a romantic hero, until the reconciliation.
actor_transformation: After rescuing Vicky and Sweetie, Amit accepts Pinky, stops Anjali from leaving and admits he loves her.
female_transformation: From hiding her daughter to acknowledging her, even at the cost of leaving her husband.
relationship_outcome: A tearful reconciliation in which both admit their love.
relationship_analysis: The marriage exposes Amit's double standard: still bitter about his own lost love, he condemns Anjali's premarital past until a crisis makes him accept Pinky. The film rewards reconciliation, but his punitive silence reads as emotional coercion today.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Unclear; Amit wants to marry her
how_they_meet: Not described in the fetched sources.
courtship_pattern: Amit insists on marrying Rekha although she says plainly that she does not want to marry but to dance and see the world (MemsaabStory).
emotional_dynamic: Pressure and resentment: Rekha feels trapped, and her success makes Amit insecure.
pair_conflict: Rekha's wish for a career against Amit's insecurity, drinking and neglect.
pair_friction_explanation: An unwanted marriage, Amit's drinking and neglect, and his later anger at her fame make the relationship openly damaged.
external_opposition_explanation: Ranjit feeds the rift, pushes Amit off a train and manages Rekha's career for his own profit.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit is an insecure husband and then an avenger, not a romantic hero.
female_transformation: From an unwilling bride to a successful film star, Sunita Devi, who is then made to accept Amit's reproaches.
relationship_outcome: Reunited after Amit's adoptive mother intervenes.
relationship_analysis: The film casts Rekha as the wife who must be forgiven, although, as MemsaabStory notes, she never betrays Amit and has no part in Ranjit's attack. From a modern perspective the marriage is coercive from the start: her refusal is overridden, and her independent success is treated as a fault.
critical_reading: MemsaabStory (2010) reads the film as a stifling, conservative story in which a woman who wants her own career is portrayed as selfish, shallow and bad.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Not described; the bachchansir blog says they meet and are attracted to each other.
courtship_pattern: Brief; they soon marry.
emotional_dynamic: Chanda wants him to give up violence, and he agrees.
pair_conflict: His violent life (a criminal don's, per the bachchansir blog).
pair_friction_explanation: Chanda is appalled by the fear he inspires and asks him to change; he agrees, so the disagreement is settled quickly.
external_opposition_explanation: A false murder charge drives the couple to a distant village, where he tries to live honestly.
lover_boy_explanation: Marriage motivates his attempt at an honest life, but the friendship with Shera and the fight against the villains dominate.
actor_transformation: Marriage prompts him to try to lead an honest, non-violent life.
relationship_outcome: Married; the fetched sources do not describe the couple at the end.
relationship_analysis: A reforming-wife pairing: Chanda's disapproval of his violence pushes him towards an honest life, which the plot then tests. The two fetched summaries disagree about how criminal he was.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Unclear
how_they_meet: Not described in the fetched sources; Radhakumari is the sister of Ganesh, and both are poor.
courtship_pattern: Love is declared through classical song rather than dialogue (ABP Live).
emotional_dynamic: Warm and mutual; they share news of expecting a child through song and imagery.
pair_conflict: None described.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Radha is lower class and Alok has been thrown out by his wealthy father for his chosen life; the fetched sources do not say the father opposes the match itself.
lover_boy_explanation: Music and the conflict with his father define Alok; the romance is a gentle secondary thread.
chemistry_explanation: ABP Live says the chemistry and build-up between Rekha and Bachchan feel natural through the classical renditions.
relationship_outcome: They have a son (cast list); the fetched sources do not describe the ending.
relationship_analysis: The romance is expressed through music and crosses class lines, in keeping with Alok's rejection of his father's world. ABP Live nonetheless calls Rekha's character merely ornamental.
critical_reading: ABP Live praises the pair's natural chemistry but finds Rekha's role ornamental.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Anthony falls head over heels for Jenny at Easter Sunday services after she returns from abroad.
courtship_pattern: Love at first sight; the fetched sources describe little courtship before the rescue.
emotional_dynamic: Comic, ardent pursuit on Anthony's side.
pair_conflict: None described.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Jenny's bodyguard Zebisco delivers her to her father, the crime lord Robert, in exchange for her hand, forcing a wedding that Anthony and Amar break up in disguise.
lover_boy_explanation: Anthony's love-struck pursuit is a major comic thread, but the family reunion and the fight against Robert dominate.
female_transformation: From Kishanlal's ward, raised as his 'niece', to a woman freed from a forced marriage.
relationship_outcome: The brothers and their sweethearts drive off together.
relationship_analysis: The pairing is played for comedy and rescue: Jenny is a prize contested by villains and saved by the hero's disguise. Rediff's remark that the heroines are basically required to sing and dance fits her limited agency.
critical_reading: Rediff (2003) says the three heroines play second fiddle and are basically required to sing and dance, though Parveen Babi looks the most fetching of the three.

initial_relationship: Strangers: a police inspector and a pickpocket
how_they_meet: Amit and Kishen encounter the orphaned pickpocketing sisters Neetu and Shabbo.
courtship_pattern: Smitten with Amit, Neetu half-heartedly resolves to go straight to win him; he gives her a locket.
emotional_dynamic: Attraction across the law, with Neetu reforming for love.
pair_conflict: Her life as a pickpocket against his duty as a police officer.
pair_friction_explanation: The inspector–pickpocket mismatch is eased by her half-hearted reform; no serious quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Mangal Singh, who killed Neetu's parents, captures and holds her hostage.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is a lighter strand beside Amit's duty, his foster brother's crimes and the truth about his parentage.
female_transformation: From a pickpocket to a woman who tries to avenge her parents and marries a police officer.
relationship_outcome: Married at the end.
relationship_analysis: The locket Amit gives Neetu makes the romance a plot device, revealing his parentage to Mangal. Neetu's attempt to kill her parents' murderer gives her initiative of her own.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Lovers
how_they_meet: Professor Amit and Suman are already in love when the story begins; his brother Raju already calls her 'Bhabhi'.
courtship_pattern: They plan to marry, but Amit has promised his mother to wait until Raju graduates (Post-Punk Cinema Club).
emotional_dynamic: A settled, affectionate partnership that shares in spoiling Raju.
pair_conflict: None; the delayed marriage troubles both.
pair_friction_explanation: They agree to wait; no quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: The promise to Amit's mother delays the wedding, and Amit is killed rescuing Raju from bad company.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit is a devoted fiancé, but responsibility for his brother shapes his story.
relationship_outcome: Amit is killed; Suman wears a widow's garb and resolves never to marry.
relationship_analysis: Their love is defined by duty to Raju: the marriage waits on his graduation, and Amit dies saving him. Suman's widowhood without a wedding carries her devotion into the second half.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; Shankar, Bachchan's second role, is her dead fiancé's look-alike
how_they_meet: Raju brings Shankar, a wanted car thief who looks exactly like Amit, into his and Suman's lives.
courtship_pattern: Raju hires Shankar and burns Suman's portraits of Amit; Raju's and Suman's affection wins Shankar away from crime (Wikipedia; Post-Punk Cinema Club).
emotional_dynamic: Suman's initial unease gives way to accepting Shankar in Amit's place.
pair_conflict: Suman's grief for Amit and Shankar's criminal past.
pair_friction_explanation: Suman is troubled by the substitution at first, and Shankar's past stands between them, but no open quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Shankar is wanted by the police, and his old criminal boss kidnaps Suman to force him to smuggle diamonds.
lover_boy_explanation: Shankar is won over by belonging as much as by love; reform and action dominate his arc.
actor_transformation: From a loner car thief to a reformed man who takes Amit's place in the family.
female_transformation: From a self-declared widow to Shankar's partner.
relationship_outcome: United; the Post-Punk Cinema Club reads Shankar's blood smeared on Suman's forehead as a symbolic marriage.
relationship_analysis: The second romance is a substitution engineered by Raju's guilt: Suman is steered towards a man who looks like her dead fiancé. The film presents this as a happy restoration; the Post-Punk Cinema Club's sardonic summary points out how little choice Suman is given.
critical_reading: The Post-Punk Cinema Club (2007) mocks the plotting that leaves Suman 'no choice left but to marry Shankar'.

initial_relationship: Business contacts: she is his father's secretary
how_they_meet: Vijay crosses paths with Geeta, R. K. Gupta's devoted secretary, and tries to bribe her for details of Gupta's tender bids.
courtship_pattern: She refuses the bribe and is furious; after Vijay apologises, clears her name and hires her, months in his company draw her to him, and he comes to depend on her (Conversations Over Chai).
emotional_dynamic: Geeta is his friend, confidante and conscience; he admits his loneliness only to her.
pair_conflict: Vijay's ruthless revenge, which distresses Geeta.
pair_friction_explanation: The bribe attempt starts them badly, and Geeta is distressed by his scheme to break up Shekhar and Sheetal, but she remains his support.
external_opposition_explanation: Gupta's suspicion, planted by Bhandari after he sees Vijay and Geeta together, costs Geeta her job.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay is organised around revenge; his need for Geeta surfaces only in one admission of loneliness.
actor_transformation: Through Geeta he finds some solace and finally turns to her 'for friendship, for affection, for love' (Conversations Over Chai).
female_transformation: From Gupta's loyal, wrongly dismissed secretary to Vijay's confidante, who reveals to Shekhar that Vijay is his brother.
relationship_outcome: Close at the end; the fetched sources do not describe a marriage.
relationship_analysis: Geeta is the voice of Vijay's conscience rather than a romantic prize: she refuses his bribe, questions his obsession and reveals his parentage to Shekhar. The reviewer finds her a deeper character than Hema Malini's larger role.
critical_reading: Conversations Over Chai says Raakhee's Geeta had more depth than Hema Malini's role despite less screen time, and describes her as Vijay's support and conscience.

initial_relationship: Enemies: she believes he is Don, who killed her brother
how_they_meet: Roma infiltrates Don's gang to avenge her brother Ramesh and his fiancée Kamini, and meets Vijay posing as Don.
courtship_pattern: Vijay begins to fall in love with Roma; when she tries to kill him he reveals he is Vijay, and she falls in love with him (Conversations Over Chai).
emotional_dynamic: Hostility turns into alliance and love as they face the police and the gang together.
pair_conflict: Roma's plan to kill the man she believes is Don.
pair_friction_explanation: She intends to kill him until she learns who he is; after that they work together.
external_opposition_explanation: Vardhaan exposes Roma to the gang and holds the children hostage, while the police hunt Vijay as Don.
lover_boy_explanation: Survival and proving his identity drive Vijay; the romance is secondary.
female_transformation: From an avenger trained in judo and karate to Vijay's ally.
relationship_outcome: They leave the police station together after Vardhaan's arrest.
relationship_analysis: Roma has her own revenge plan and the skills to carry it out, which gives her unusual initiative in the pairing. The romance grows out of mistaken identity into a partnership against the gang.
critical_reading: Conversations Over Chai calls the pair's duet Jiska mujhe tha intezaar the film's only false note, a 'regulation duet' added because Zeenat Aman had been signed.

initial_relationship: Childhood friends across class: she is his employer's daughter
how_they_meet: As an orphan boy working in Ramnath's house, Sikandar is befriended by Ramnath's young daughter Kaamna.
courtship_pattern: He secretly pays her family's bills, then sends a love letter written by Vishal, which Kaamna takes to be from Vishal.
emotional_dynamic: Silent devotion on his side; indifference and rebuff on hers, as she tells him never to speak to her again.
pair_conflict: Kaamna's rejection and the misattributed letter.
pair_friction_explanation: Kaamna snubs his offers and tells him never to speak to her; the rest of the distance is his silence rather than conflict.
external_opposition_explanation: Ramnath's hatred of the orphan, Kaamna's engagement to Sikandar's best friend, and Dilawar's kidnapping of Kaamna, which leads to Sikandar's fatal fight.
lover_boy_explanation: Sikandar's lifelong, unspoken love for Kaamna is his defining trait, and he dies revealing it.
actor_transformation: Rejection drives Sikandar to drink and to Zohra's brothel; he gives Kaamna up to Vishal and dies saving her from Dilawar.
female_transformation: From a rich man's daughter whose family falls on hard times to Vishal's bride.
relationship_outcome: Kaamna marries Vishal; Sikandar dies at the wedding.
relationship_analysis: ThePrint reads the story as a reworking of Devdas in which the heroine, unlike Paro, has no interest in the hero. The film ennobles renunciation: Sikandar hides his love to secure his friend's happiness.
critical_reading: ThePrint notes that Kaamna has no interest in Sikandar, which it calls one of the film's major deviations from Devdas.

initial_relationship: Courtesan and client
how_they_meet: Heartbroken over Kaamna, Sikandar begins visiting Zohra Begum's brothel.
courtship_pattern: Zohra falls in love with Sikandar and refuses other clients.
emotional_dynamic: Her devotion against his need for her company without love.
pair_conflict: Sikandar does not love her.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is described; the gap is his emotional unavailability.
external_opposition_explanation: Mehroo's marriage is threatened by Sikandar's visits, Vishal asks Zohra to give him up, the criminal Dilawar loves her, and she dies.
lover_boy_explanation: Sikandar never loves Zohra, as Dilawar learns only at the end.
female_transformation: From a courtesan to a woman who refuses other clients and Vishal's money for Sikandar's sake, then dies.
relationship_outcome: Zohra dies before the climax.
relationship_analysis: Zohra is the film's Chandramukhi (ThePrint): the courtesan whose love for the hero is selfless and unreturned. She gives him up to protect Mehroo's marriage; the film grants her dignity but no reciprocity.
critical_reading: ThePrint identifies Zohra Begum as the film's version of Devdas's Chandramukhi.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is sent to seduce the man she believes is Vijay
how_they_meet: Shabnam and her boyfriend Romesh mistake Jai for Vijay at the airline counter and arrange for her to sit beside him on the flight to Rome via Cairo.
courtship_pattern: Flirting on the flight and a day of wining and dining in Cairo, engineered by the gang.
emotional_dynamic: A pleasant flirtation built on her deception; once the gang traps Jai, his contempt 'sears her'.
pair_conflict: Shabnam's role as the gang's bait, which leads to Jai being trapped and coerced.
pair_friction_explanation: Her deception and his open contempt after he is coerced create real hostility, following an easy flirtation.
external_opposition_explanation: Saxena's gang uses the relationship as a trap, and Shabnam is Romesh's girlfriend, whom he intends to marry.
lover_boy_explanation: Jai flirts readily, but money and survival drive him.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Shabnam is the gang's bait, sent by her own boyfriend's boss to make the man she thinks is Vijay fall for her. The flirtation is enjoyable for both until Jai is trapped, and his contempt then exposes how the relationship was manipulated from the start.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; Mala believes Vijay is Jai, the man she is to marry
how_they_meet: Mala meets Vijay at the Rome airport and mistakes him for Jai, whom Ratan Das has arranged for her to marry.
courtship_pattern: Mala shows 'Jai' around Rome and openly declares and shows her love; Vijay plays along to find out who his double is.
emotional_dynamic: Her open devotion against his growing guilt at deceiving her.
pair_conflict: Vijay's impersonation of Jai.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel is described; the strain is Vijay's conscience over the deception.
external_opposition_explanation: Mala is promised to Jai in a marriage arranged for her father's fortune, and Vijay's case against Saxena pulls him away.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay is 'not immune to her charms', but his mission comes first.
relationship_outcome: Vijay leaves for Rome with a note confessing he is not the real Jai; the fetched sources stop there.
relationship_analysis: Mala gives her love to a man she has misidentified. The romance is mostly a complication of the double role, though Vijay's confession note shows the deception weighing on him.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the daughter of Inder's former college professor
how_they_meet: Inder meets Rama at Pratapgarh through her father, his college professor Daya Shankar Sharma.
courtship_pattern: A calculated pursuit to win a bet with Prakash; when his tricks fail, he publishes a book of her poems for her.
emotional_dynamic: A cynical wager that turns into guilt and devotion on his side; Rama is won over by the gift of her poems.
pair_conflict: Inder's belief that money can buy any woman, and the lie Rama tells to be with him, which exposes her to her father's scorn.
pair_friction_explanation: His mercenary wager ruins her standing, and their reunion requires 'misunderstandings and differences' to be settled.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father scorns her and she leaves home; a robbery and a train accident then leave her presumed dead.
lover_boy_explanation: Courtship dominates his arc, first as a wager and then as a guilty search, but it is not simple devotion.
actor_transformation: From a man who treats a woman as a bet to one driven by guilt to find her.
female_transformation: From a sheltered professor's daughter to a renowned singer living on her own.
relationship_outcome: Inder hears her on the radio, finds her, and they come together.
relationship_analysis: The relationship begins as a transaction, a bet that women can be bought, and Rama pays for it with her home and reputation. The film redeems Inder through guilt and searching; a modern reading would weigh the wager and the damage to Rama against the easy reunion.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; Natwar arrives in her village disguised as a hunter
how_they_meet: In Chandanpur, where Natwar arrives posing as the hunter Avtar Singh.
courtship_pattern: Shanno 'sets her cap at' the stranger, who lingers in the village; he rescues her from Vikram's men and she rescues him in turn.
emotional_dynamic: Funny and direct on her side, with mutual rescues.
pair_conflict: None described; the obstacles come from Vikram.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Vikram's gang threatens her, and she is held captive at his diamond mine.
lover_boy_explanation: Revenge drives Natwar; Shanno is a welcome distraction rather than his goal.
chemistry_explanation: Cinema Chaat (blog) calls their chemistry 'always wonderful' and says Rekha's funny, direct Shanno brings the relationship to life despite its 'insta-love'.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Shanno is an active heroine who chooses the stranger and rescues him as often as he rescues her. The romance is a light counterweight to Natwar's revenge plot.
critical_reading: Cinema Chaat (2016) says Shanno 'appears to fall for insta-love', but that Rekha plays her 'funny and direct' and gives her 'fire and resolve'.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the mining town's new doctor
how_they_meet: Vijay is brought to her clinic after being trapped in the mine, and frustrates her by refusing anaesthesia.
courtship_pattern: Unspoken: she shares her story, he is touched, and they slowly come to understand each other until 'they know they are in love'.
emotional_dynamic: Restrained; Sudha tries to make the guilt-ridden Vijay face his past.
pair_conflict: His guilt and self-punishment, which keep him closed off.
pair_friction_explanation: Her frustration at his refusal of anaesthesia is the only friction described.
external_opposition_explanation: His haunted past and the dangers of the mine, rather than any person, stand between them.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay's arc is guilt and atonement; the romance is 'subtle and understated'.
actor_transformation: Sudha helps him begin to face his past.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: A quiet romance between two people with private histories; Sudha offers emotional and moral support to a man defined by guilt.
critical_reading: Conversations Over Chai (blog) compares the subtle, understated romance with Bachchan and Raakhee's pairing in Trishul.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: At a friend's wedding, according to the bachchansir blog.
courtship_pattern: Ajay courts the wealthy Aruna while pretending to be rich with a borrowed suit, car and flat; she returns his feelings.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual affection; after his confession Aruna is sympathetic and loves him for who he is.
pair_conflict: Ajay's pretence of wealth.
pair_friction_explanation: The deception could have broken them, but Aruna responds with sympathy.
external_opposition_explanation: Her lawyer father throws Ajay out, rejects the marriage proposal and prosecutes him for fraud.
lover_boy_explanation: His ambition is partly about deserving Aruna, but his business and his mother share the story.
actor_transformation: From faking wealth to winning her father's approval through honest work.
relationship_outcome: Ajay wins over Aruna's father once his name is cleared (bachchansir blog).
relationship_analysis: The romance prompts Ajay's lie and survives it. Aruna's support and her father's class-based hostility frame his move from pretence to honest enterprise.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Established attachment; Amit already loves Basanti, a nautch girl whose kotha he frequents
how_they_meet: Not shown in the fetched sources; the attachment already exists when adult Amit is introduced.
courtship_pattern: On each visit, often drunk and rowdy, Amit urges her to leave the business and marry him; she refuses, in what the blog calls 'a mutual long-standing ritual'.
emotional_dynamic: Affectionate sparring; Basanti is practical, smelling his breath before agreeing to help him.
pair_conflict: Her refusal to give up the kotha and marry him; his drinking.
pair_friction_explanation: Their disagreement is a recurring, good-humoured ritual rather than a rupture.
external_opposition_explanation: Her profession and his criminal, alcoholic life stand in the way; the blog wonders how her sister Annu will react to her work.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit's pursuit of Basanti is persistent, but friendship with Kishan and revenge dominate his role.
chemistry_explanation: Conversations Over Chai (blog) says Rekha 'had great chemistry with the Bachchan. The sparks just flew'.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Basanti is a strong, practical masala heroine who holds her own against Amit's proposals. The relationship is comic and affectionate, secondary to the brothers' story.
critical_reading: Conversations Over Chai (2018) calls Rekha 'a great masala heroine – strong, feminine, beautiful'; one of its two writers found Amit a 'sanctimonious prick' at one point.

initial_relationship: Strangers; Vijay is posing as the PE instructor Ram
how_they_meet: At the school, where Anju is the principal's daughter.
courtship_pattern: Anju falls in love with 'Ram' without knowing he is a burglar.
emotional_dynamic: When she learns the truth, her love and affection help reform him.
pair_conflict: His false identity and criminal purpose.
pair_friction_explanation: Discovering his identity is a mild rupture that ends in his reform.
external_opposition_explanation: The kidnapping plot and his criminal bosses are the only obstacles described.
lover_boy_explanation: The comic rivalry and the child dominate; the romance is incidental.
actor_transformation: Anju's love helps change him for good.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Anju serves as the reforming influence and reward for the crook. A 2008 blog review says both heroines are sidelined.
critical_reading: Post-Punk Cinema Club (2008) calls Hema Malini and Parveen Babi 'wonderfully cheeky, charismatic superstars' relegated to 'the most menial of supporting roles'.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Vijay and Ravi each meet Sheetal separately, at different places and times.
courtship_pattern: Vijay's love is 'more vocal' and she returns it; Ravi's crush is one-sided.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual love strained by Vijay's loyalty to Ravi.
pair_conflict: Vijay's decision to give her up for Ravi's sake.
pair_friction_explanation: The rupture comes from Vijay's sacrifice and Daaga's scheming, not from quarrels between the couple.
external_opposition_explanation: Ravi's love for Sheetal, Daaga's use of a photograph to set the friends against each other, and Ravi's demand that she spend a night with him in return for defending Vijay.
lover_boy_explanation: Love and sacrifice for love shape Vijay's arc, alongside friendship and the crime plot.
relationship_outcome: Ravi repents after reading Vijay's letter; the fetched plot does not say how the couple ends up.
relationship_analysis: The triangle puts Sheetal's choice below the men's friendship: Vijay renounces her for Ravi, Daaga uses their relationship as a weapon, and Ravi bargains for her body in exchange for defending Vijay. The film frames the renunciation as noble; a modern reading notes how little say Sheetal has.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Rivals; both are thieves after the same necklace
how_they_meet: At a hotel party, Sunita steals the Maharani's necklace first and slips it into Vijay's pocket during the police search.
courtship_pattern: After she helps him escape with the necklace hidden in his walking stick, Vijay falls for her and invites her into his gang.
emotional_dynamic: Partners in crime, and later in the mission against Shakaal.
pair_conflict: Only their first rivalry over the necklace.
pair_friction_explanation: The necklace trick is a playful rivalry that turns straight into partnership.
external_opposition_explanation: Police arrests and Shakaal's island put the couple in danger, though not specifically as a couple.
lover_boy_explanation: Vijay is a con man and avenger first; the romance is a side-strand.
relationship_outcome: They escape Shakaal's exploding island together by helicopter.
relationship_analysis: A caper romance between equals: Sunita outwits the con men at their own game and later helps infiltrate Shakaal's island, posing as a dancer.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she is the blind daughter of the tea-estate manager Suresh (Boro Babu)
how_they_meet: Abhijeet meets Rajni while living incognito in the tea-estate area.
courtship_pattern: Abhijeet falls in love with Rajni and rescues her when Kaaliram tries to molest her on a rainy night.
emotional_dynamic: Protective love that becomes a harmonious marriage.
pair_conflict: None described.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between the couple is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Kaaliram attempts to molest Rajni and later attacks her at home while she is pregnant, causing a miscarriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Abhijeet is foremost a crusading officer; the marriage gives his mission a personal cost.
relationship_outcome: Married and living in Sonarpur; Kaaliram's attack costs them their unborn child.
relationship_analysis: Rajni is defined by vulnerability and is twice the target of Kaaliram's violence. The marriage is loving, but the film uses her suffering to drive Abhijeet's pursuit of justice.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; Asha is a singer
how_they_meet: Johnny arrives in time to rescue Asha when her boss's son Ashok threatens her.
courtship_pattern: Their romance 'flourishes' with 'complete understanding'; Johnny even mistakes her ad shoot for real life, and never asks her to give up her show.
emotional_dynamic: Equal and unselfconscious; Asha is not coy and feels she can take on his 'mehboob'.
pair_conflict: Johnny's staged sacrifice of their love for Vicky's sake.
pair_friction_explanation: The staged sacrifice leaves Asha 'furious', though she later understands why he did it.
external_opposition_explanation: Vicky loves Asha too, Damu arranges Vicky's marriage to her, and the villains threaten the whole family.
lover_boy_explanation: Johnny is an open, devoted lover whose sacrifice for friendship is the film's emotional centre, shared with the revenge plot.
chemistry_explanation: Conversations Over Chai (blog) praises the couple's 'complete understanding of each other' and says 'Romances should be like this'.
relationship_outcome: Vicky steps aside and hands Asha over to Johnny (Conversations Over Chai).
relationship_analysis: Asha is a working singer who keeps her career and is not coy. The triangle tests Johnny's loyalty to Vicky, and the film resolves it by having Vicky hand her back 'like a parcel', as the blog puts it.
critical_reading: Conversations Over Chai (2022) holds the romance up as a model but mocks Vicky returning Asha to Johnny 'like a parcel'.

initial_relationship: Strangers as adults; the BRNS review says she once gave him a book as a girl
how_they_meet: Heera comes across Mohini, a privileged woman, and pursues her; she turns out to be the girl who gave him a book in childhood (BRNS review).
courtship_pattern: Heera 'stalks her to show his affection' (BRNS); Mohini falls in love with him without knowing his true identity (Wikipedia).
emotional_dynamic: Attraction across a class divide.
pair_conflict: The class gap and his unknown parentage.
pair_friction_explanation: Her early airs and his pursuit suggest mild friction; no serious quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Their class difference and Mahendar Singh's attempts to kill Heera.
lover_boy_explanation: The romance is secondary to Heera's search for identity and his fight with Mahendar.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: The pursuit is framed as romantic persistence across class. A modern reading would treat the stalking described in the BRNS review as a red flag. The romance stays secondary to Heera's search for a father.
critical_reading: The BRNS review describes the pursuit sardonically ('and of course stalks her').

initial_relationship: Strangers who become lovers; later she is married to Dr. Anand
how_they_meet: Amit meets Chandni while his brother Shekhar is engaged to Shobha; their relationship 'blossoms into love' before he can introduce her to Shekhar.
courtship_pattern: A brief, happy courtship; her parents almost arrange her wedding on learning of her love for Amit (bachchansir blog).
emotional_dynamic: Passionate and poetic at first, later secretive and guilt-ridden.
pair_conflict: Amit's letter ending the relationship after he marries Shobha, and later the choice between their affair and their marriages.
pair_friction_explanation: His abandonment by letter breaks her heart, and the renewed affair ends when Chandni returns to her husband.
external_opposition_source: Existing relationship; War or politics; Family
external_opposition_explanation: Shekhar's death in the 1971 war leads Amit to marry Shobha; both lovers are then married, and Shobha's policeman cousin threatens to expose the affair.
lover_boy_explanation: Amit is a romantic poet-playwright whose identity centres on his love for Chandni, though he twice chooses duty over her.
chemistry_explanation: Sunil Sethi (India Today, 1981) found Rekha's 'mixture of passion and guilt' unconvincing and Bachchan's seduction 'synthetic'; later popular memory of the pairing was not assessed in fetched sources.
actor_transformation: From a devoted lover to a husband of duty, then an adulterer who returns to his marriage.
female_transformation: From Amit's beloved to Anand's wife and Amit's secret lover, who finally recommits to her husband.
relationship_outcome: Chandni realises she loves her husband and returns to him; Amit returns to Shobha.
relationship_analysis: The film treats Amit and Chandni's love as the true passion and marriage as the claim that wins. Adultery is dramatised sympathetically but closed off by the ending, and both women's choices are shaped by the men's decisions about duty.
critical_reading: Sunil Sethi (India Today, 1981) argued that Yash Chopra 'reconventionalised' adultery and that Bachchan's seduction of Rekha was 'as synthetic as his tiresome chauvinism'. Rachel Dwyer, cited by Wikipedia, found Bachchan's angry-young-man persona incompatible with the lover's role.

initial_relationship: His brother's fiancée and a friend
how_they_meet: Shekhar introduces Amit to his fiancée Shobha, and the three become close.
courtship_pattern: No courtship; after Shekhar's death Amit marries the pregnant Shobha to shield her from scorn and honour his brother.
emotional_dynamic: A marriage of duty; Shobha comes to revere and love Amit, while he remains devoted to Chandni.
pair_conflict: Amit's affair and his decision to leave the loveless marriage.
pair_friction_explanation: The marriage is passionless after the miscarriage, and Amit's affair and plan to leave shatter Shobha.
external_opposition_explanation: Shekhar's death, the car accident that ends her pregnancy, and Amit's continuing love for Chandni.
lover_boy_explanation: Here Amit is a dutiful and then unfaithful husband, not a lover.
chemistry_explanation: Sethi (India Today, 1981) called Amit's 'sacrifice to marry Jaya' synthetic and mocked Jaya's tearful scene as he prepares to leave.
actor_transformation: Returns to the marriage after the plane crash, when Shobha tells him she is carrying his child.
female_transformation: From Shekhar's grieving, pregnant fiancée to a wife who genuinely loves Amit and wins him back.
relationship_outcome: Amit returns to Shobha, who is expecting his child; the film ends with them happy in their marriage.
relationship_analysis: Marriage here is duty rather than romance: Amit marries Shobha to protect her, neglects and betrays her, and returns when she is pregnant and Chandni has left. The film presents the ending as restoration; a modern reading sees Shobha's patience rewarded by a husband who has not freely chosen her.
critical_reading: Sethi (India Today, 1981) called the ending an 'affirmation of marriage' reached through 'filmi touches' and asked whether it could be so easy.

initial_relationship: Tutor and reluctant pupil
how_they_meet: Bishan asks Komal, the daughter of Kishan's singing teacher, to groom Kishan into a performer and a gentleman.
courtship_pattern: Kishan resists her grooming by being uncooperative; she gives him 'a little romantic encouragement' before the concert and declares her love after his success.
emotional_dynamic: From exasperated tutor and unruly pupil to affection.
pair_conflict: Kishan's disruptive behaviour during his training.
pair_friction_explanation: His deliberate disruptions cause mild, largely comic friction.
external_opposition_explanation: No external obstacle to the couple is described.
lover_boy_explanation: Friendship with Bishan drives Kishan; the romance is a side-strand.
relationship_outcome: Komal declares her love once Kishan becomes a star; the fetched sources do not describe their future.
relationship_analysis: The romance is a side-strand in a friendship film. Komal's function is to polish the rustic hero and encourage him, part of the formula the India Today review describes.
critical_reading: India Today's reviewer (1981) mentions Neetu Singh only as supplying 'a little romantic encouragement'.

initial_relationship: Strangers; a Letterboxd review describes her as a bar dancer used by Shahani
how_they_meet: Not described; Wikipedia says only that after his release Kaalia 'pairs up with' Shalini.
courtship_pattern: Comic domestic moments: Kaalia shows her how to wear a sari, and she tries to cook an omelette (Letterboxd review).
emotional_dynamic: Light companionship inside a revenge story.
pair_conflict: Not described.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Shahani, who sent her after a diamond and who turns out to have kidnapped her as a child, is the couple's enemy.
lover_boy_explanation: Revenge defines Kaalia; the romance supplies light relief.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources; Shalini is revealed as the jailer Raghuvir's kidnapped daughter.
relationship_analysis: Shalini is a 'bad girl' dancer with her own hidden identity. The romance adds comic domestic scenes rather than shaping Kaalia's revenge.
critical_reading: No professional review was fetched; a Letterboxd user review enjoys the sari and omelette scenes.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Trying to persuade Nurse Sheela to marry his friend Shekhar, Ravi lectures the wrong woman, Indu (bachchansir blog).
courtship_pattern: Indu dislikes his filth and manners, so Ravi shaves, dresses up and woos her, pretending he has only one younger brother.
emotional_dynamic: From disgust to affection; after the wedding she takes charge of the household and becomes pregnant.
pair_conflict: Ravi's uncouth ways and his concealment of five of his brothers.
pair_friction_explanation: Her dislike before the wedding and the shock of his hidden brothers after it cause real friction.
external_opposition_explanation: Ranjit Singh has Ravi kidnapped and replaced by his lookalike Babu.
lover_boy_explanation: Winning Indu drives the first half and transforms Ravi, but family comedy and the crime plot share the film.
actor_transformation: Ravi grooms himself into a presentable suitor.
female_transformation: From a disapproving nurse to the mother figure who civilises seven brothers.
relationship_outcome: Reunited after Ravi defeats Ranjit.
relationship_analysis: Indu civilises Ravi and his brothers, reversing the usual taming plot. The deception about the brothers is played for comedy, and her authority in the house brings order to the film.
critical_reading: Jagannath Dubashi (India Today, 1982) calls Bachchan and Hema Malini 'the first brother and the first bride' of the Seven Brides copy and says the wife 'soon sets house and brothers to rights'.

initial_relationship: Hired killer and intended victim
how_they_meet: Posing as Ravi at the farmhouse, Babu is about to stab Seema when the shock restores her ability to walk.
courtship_pattern: Overcome with guilt at the family's happiness, Babu falls in love with Seema, who falls for him too.
emotional_dynamic: Redemptive love; Seema loses the use of her legs again when he tries to leave.
pair_conflict: Babu's mission to murder her.
pair_friction_explanation: He begins as her would-be murderer, even though she does not know it.
external_opposition_explanation: Seema's uncle Ranjit Singh hires Babu to kill her for her inheritance.
lover_boy_explanation: Love is what redeems Babu, but it arrives late in the film.
actor_transformation: From hired killer to penitent lover who helps rescue Ravi.
female_transformation: From a wheelchair-bound heiress to a woman who walks again.
relationship_outcome: Babu uses his dagger to make her stand up from her wheelchair, and they stay together.
relationship_analysis: The romance redeems the double: Babu's love turns the murder plot into a cure. Because Seema's recovery depends on him, she has little agency of her own.
critical_reading: Dubashi (India Today, 1982) says Babu 'falls for her with a thud'; Rediff (2003) says he 'finds love with the very lady he was sent to kill'.

initial_relationship: Strangers met on holiday
how_they_meet: Sudhir and Prashant meet Kavita Goel on holiday and keep seeing her.
courtship_pattern: Though interested himself, Sudhir recommends Prashant to her; when she asks why he will not marry her, he cites his brother's mental illness and his criminal past.
emotional_dynamic: Suppressed attraction turned into protective friendship.
pair_conflict: Sudhir's refusal to marry her.
pair_friction_explanation: Her question and his refusal are handled calmly; no quarrel is described.
external_opposition_explanation: His fear of hereditary mental illness, his past as a thief, and Prashant's claim on Kavita.
lover_boy_explanation: Sudhir's defining trait is self-sacrifice for his foster family, not romance.
relationship_outcome: Kavita marries Prashant; Sudhir remains the family's protector and takes the blame for Prashant's crime.
