relationship_analysis: Giving up Kavita is the first of Sudhir's sacrifices for the family that adopted him. The romance exists to show his self-denial.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers thrown together in a group wedding
how_they_meet: Running from the police, Raju hides in a group wedding beside Asha, a cabaret dancer fleeing a cruel stepbrother (Memsaabstory).
courtship_pattern: Raju wants her gone, but she treats the accidental wedding as a lifelong commitment and follows him singing 'Jaoji Jao'; he spends the wedding night with her in a seedy hotel and disappears before she wakes.
emotional_dynamic: Her determined devotion against his evasion.
pair_conflict: Raju's desertion after the wedding night.
pair_friction_explanation: He abandons her while she insists on the marriage.
external_opposition_explanation: Her cruel stepbrother and Raju's criminal life with Pratap Singh.
lover_boy_explanation: Raju is a rogue who evades commitment; romance is incidental to his crimes.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources; Memsaabstory asks whether Asha will ever find her new husband.
relationship_analysis: The comic 'marriage' makes Asha the pursuer and Raju the cad. His desertion after the wedding night is played lightly within the patriotic melodrama.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: At the five-star hotel where Arjun works as a bellboy.
courtship_pattern: They fall in love; the rain duet 'Aaj Rapat Jaayen To' is their best-known song.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual affection; the fetched sources say little more.
pair_conflict: None described.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the couple is described.
external_opposition_explanation: Ranjit's goons kidnap the families, including those close to Arjun, in the finale.
lover_boy_explanation: Arjun's loyalty to Raja and his comic persona dominate; the romance is a side-strand.
relationship_outcome: Arjun marries Poonam at the end.
relationship_analysis: Poonam is a conventional heroine in a loyalty-and-comedy film. Off screen, Smita Patil, known for art-house work, was uncomfortable with the song-and-dance role and needed Bachchan's persuasion to perform the rain song.
critical_reading: ThePrint (2024) reports that Patil went home and cried after shooting 'Aaj Rapat Jaayen To', and quotes Bachchan's 2016 blog saying she was uncomfortable throughout; the Indian Express (2022) says he put her at ease.

initial_relationship: Unclear
how_they_meet: Not described in the fetched sources.
courtship_pattern: Mary, a Christian woman in the illicit liquor trade, gives it up to win Govind over (India Today).
emotional_dynamic: Reform through love: Govind's values change her.
pair_conflict: Her illicit liquor business against his honesty.
pair_friction_explanation: The clash of values is resolved by her giving up the trade.
external_opposition_explanation: No external obstacle to the couple is described.
lover_boy_explanation: Govind's role centres on his brothers and his pride; the romance is minor.
female_transformation: Gives up the illicit liquor trade to win Govind.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Mary is one of the people the hero reforms; in the fetched sources her change of trade is the romance's whole arc.
critical_reading: S. Venkat Narayan (India Today, 1982) counts Parveen Babi's character among those Bachchan's hero 'goes about reforming'.

initial_relationship: Strangers
how_they_meet: Vijay rescues Roma from four men trying to molest her.
courtship_pattern: They grow close; after his father throws him out, Vijay moves in with Roma without marrying her, and marries her when she becomes pregnant.
emotional_dynamic: Roma is his refuge from the estrangement with his father.
pair_conflict: None described between them.
pair_friction_explanation: No disagreement between the couple is described.
external_opposition_explanation: His father's hostility, J.K.'s gang, a murder frame-up and finally Vijay's death at his father's hands.
lover_boy_explanation: The father-son conflict defines Vijay; Roma is a steady presence rather than his motive.
female_transformation: From a single woman living alone to Vijay's wife and the mother of Ravi.
relationship_outcome: Married; Vijay is killed by his father, and Ashwini takes Roma in (bachchansir blog).
relationship_analysis: Roma gives Vijay the home he has lost. The couple live together before marrying, and the pregnancy prompts the wedding, but the film's emotional centre is father and son.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Married couple with a young daughter
how_they_meet: Already married when the story of Khan's past begins; the fetched sources do not show how they met.
who_initiates: Not described in the fetched sources
courtship_pattern: Marital affection; India Today describes a comic song in which he tries in vain to coax a kiss on the cheek from her.
emotional_dynamic: Playful, affectionate domesticity, cut short by his imprisonment.
pair_conflict: None between them; the tragedy is imposed from outside.
pair_friction_explanation: Only her teasing refusal of a kiss in the song.
external_opposition_explanation: Ram Gupta's staged death sends Khan to prison, and while he is away she is assaulted and kills herself and their daughter.
lover_boy_explanation: A fond, teasing husband in one song; the role is defined by grief and revenge.
actor_transformation: Her death turns him from an honest officer into an avenger.
female_transformation: None; she is a victim whose death drives his story.
relationship_outcome: She kills herself and their daughter while he is in prison.
romantic_songs: A comic song in which he coaxes his wife for a kiss (India Today does not name it).
relationship_analysis: The marriage is sketched in one playful song and exists mainly to be destroyed: Zakhiya's assault and suicide turn Khan's wrongful imprisonment into a personal vendetta. A modern reading would note that her suffering serves only to motivate his revenge.
critical_reading: India Today (1983) singled out Bachchan's comic flair in the song in which he cajoles his wife 'in vain to plant a kiss on his cheek', and said the film would have done as well 'with less violence, fewer rapes and bedroom scenes'.

initial_relationship: Strangers; she recruits him for a pretend marriage
how_they_meet: Rita comes to Guru for help, asking him to stage a fake marriage to satisfy her grandfather Rai Sahab's insistence (Talking Sid).
courtship_pattern: A staged marriage that turns into real love on her side; Wikipedia says Guru is 'pursued by Rita'.
emotional_dynamic: Comic; she moves from using him as a front to loving him.
pair_conflict: The pretence at the heart of their arrangement.
pair_friction_explanation: No sourced quarrel beyond the pretence itself.
external_opposition_explanation: Her grandfather's insistence on her marriage prompts the pretence; the sources describe no active opposition to the couple.
lover_boy_explanation: Guru is the comic twin; the sources give him no romantic initiative.
female_transformation: She moves from staging a marriage to falling in love with Guru.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Rita drives this subplot: she stages a marriage with the carefree performer Guru to manage her grandfather, then falls for him. The sources say little about Guru's feelings, and the pairing is one strand of a family-reunion melodrama.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing. A search-result summary mentions over-the-top Bachchan–Zeenat scenes, but no fetched page confirms it.

initial_relationship: Disputed: Talking Sid has her raised in Janki's household with Shankar; Wikipedia makes her Rana Ranveer's adopted daughter, who meets Shankar as a stranger
how_they_meet: Wikipedia says Manju meets and falls in love with Shankar, unaware that he is her adoptive father's long-lost son; Talking Sid says she is an orphan cared for by Janki.
courtship_pattern: Her love for Shankar is stated; the fetched sources describe no courtship scenes.
emotional_dynamic: Not described beyond Manju's love.
pair_conflict: Not described in the fetched sources.
pair_friction_explanation: No sourced conflict between them.
external_opposition_explanation: Hidden family ties complicate the match: she is linked to the father Shankar believes lost, but the sources describe no active opposition.
lover_boy_explanation: Talking Sid calls Shankar the angry-young-man twin; no romantic role is described.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_analysis: Manju's love for Shankar links the two halves of the separated family, but the sources disagree about her background and describe no development of the romance.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers from opposite classes: a porter and a wealthy heiress
how_they_meet: When the coolies crash her engagement party to Vicky, Iqbal carries Julie off as a hostage; she escapes after tying him up (MemsaabStory).
who_initiates: Iqbal, by carrying her off; MemsaabStory calls it 'love at first sight'
courtship_pattern: A comic abduction and escape, then romance while she resists her guardian's marriage plan.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual attraction with playful sparring; she keeps her own aim of avenging her father.
pair_conflict: Her engagement to Vicky, and her mistaken belief that Iqbal's father Aslam killed her father.
pair_friction_explanation: The hostage-taking and escape are played as sparring, and her attempt on Aslam threatens Iqbal's family, though the sources do not say it sets her against Iqbal.
external_opposition_explanation: Her guardian Puri pushes her to marry Vicky for her fortune, and Zafar Khan's frame-up makes her target Iqbal's father.
lover_boy_explanation: Iqbal courts Julie with swagger, but the workers' cause and his mother dominate the role.
female_transformation: She drops her vendetta when Aslam explains that Zafar killed her father.
relationship_outcome: Not described in the fetched sources; the film ends with Iqbal's recovery and his family's reunion.
relationship_analysis: The romance begins with a comic abduction framed as love at first sight, which a modern reading would question. Julie is more than a prize: she resists her guardian's mercenary match and pursues her own revenge, which briefly turns her against Iqbal's father.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he is a police officer, she the only daughter of the tycoon Seetharam
how_they_meet: Wikipedia says only that Amar meets Asha and they fall for each other.
who_initiates: Not described in the fetched sources
courtship_pattern: Mutual attraction, followed by Amar persuading her father Seetharam to accept the match.
emotional_dynamic: A loving marriage that breaks when Asha misreads Amar's collaboration with the syndicate.
pair_conflict: Asha's belief that Amar has become corrupt, when he is being blackmailed by her own father's syndicate.
pair_friction_explanation: She leaves him with their newborn child, a serious rupture rooted in mistrust.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father and Amar's political mentor run the syndicate that blackmails him, and Amar ultimately kills her father.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is one strand of a political revenge story; Amar is defined by his public role.
actor_transformation: Heartbroken by the separation, he resigns from the police and enters politics.
female_transformation: She learns of her father's crimes and the blackmail, and reconciles with Amar.
relationship_outcome: They reconcile, but Amar surrenders to the police after killing the syndicate.
relationship_analysis: The marriage is caught between Amar's duty and a syndicate run by Asha's father. She leaves because she misreads his compromises, and the reconciliation comes only after he has killed her father, a cost the sources do not examine. The bachchansir blog gives a different account of her discovery.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Strangers from opposite classes: an industrialist's heir and a poor dancer
how_they_meet: Vicky meets Meena, a professional dancer and the daughter of a poor blind man, and falls in love with her.
courtship_pattern: Gifts and attention, which her greedy agent Natwar steals from her.
emotional_dynamic: Devoted and protective; he defies his father for her.
pair_conflict: Natwar frames Vicky with another woman, but the sources do not say that the frame-up turns Meena against him.
pair_friction_explanation: No quarrel between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: His father rejects a poor bride and disowns him; Natwar harasses and kidnaps her; Govardhandas pays to have her killed, and her death is faked.
lover_boy_explanation: His love for Meena is one of Vicky's main drives, alongside his bond with Phoolchand and his conflict with his father.
actor_transformation: Love for Meena, and Phoolchand's death, push him to give up alcohol.
female_transformation: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_outcome: Abdul returns Meena alive, and Amarnath welcomes her into the family.
relationship_analysis: A class romance in which Vicky chooses a poor dancer over his father's money. Nearly all the obstacles are external—his father's snobbery and the schemers who exploit it—so the romance mostly tests Vicky's loyalty, while Meena has little say in her own fate.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Fellow police inspectors
how_they_meet: Geeta is Karan's colleague; Hussein's mother urges him to propose to her, and he does.
courtship_pattern: A proposal, followed by Karan rescuing Geeta and Hussein's mother from jewellery-shop robbers.
emotional_dynamic: Warm and teasing within a trio of Karan, Geeta and Hussein, who is her rakhi brother.
pair_conflict: Geeta cautions them against abusing their uniforms, and her brother Vijay belongs to the gang Karan fights.
pair_friction_explanation: A brief argument over police methods.
external_opposition_explanation: Her brother Vijay helps murder Hussein and Karan burns him to death in revenge; her father, the Police Commissioner, warns Karan off and later nearly shoots him.
lover_boy_explanation: A single proposal in a story about revenge and a lost family.
relationship_outcome: Wikipedia says Karan marries Geeta at the end, but its account of the ending is internally inconsistent.
relationship_analysis: A small romance inside a brothers-and-revenge plot, notable for the collision it creates: Karan kills Geeta's brother to avenge Hussein. The sources do not say how Geeta responds, so the reported marriage goes unexplained.
critical_reading: No fetched review assesses the pairing.

initial_relationship: Antagonists across a class and colonial divide: a tonga driver and the spoiled daughter of a British collaborator
how_they_meet: Raju confronts Ruby over her reckless behaviour, and she falls in love with him (Wikipedia).
who_initiates: Ruby falls for Raju after he confronts her
courtship_pattern: Combative: Post-Punk Cinema Club describes them whipping each other and rubbing salt in each other's wounds before love.
emotional_dynamic: Aggressive sparring that turns into mutual loyalty.
pair_conflict: Her arrogance, and his defiance of her father's class.

emotional_dynamic: An affectionate partnership that their son's death divides over the future of their widowed daughter-in-law.
pair_conflict: Shobhna resists Balraj's plan for Millie to marry Rajat because she fears losing their grandson, Ansh.
pair_friction_explanation: A sustained disagreement over Millie's remarriage, which Balraj overcomes by persuasion.
external_opposition_explanation: His orthodox elder brother Balwant opposes widow remarriage and pressures the household, but does not threaten the marriage itself.
lover_boy_explanation: An affectionate husband; the role centres on fatherhood and social reform.
chemistry_explanation: Rediff's Sudarshana Dwivedi felt 'the relationship between AB and Hema Malini was not as spontaneous in Baabul as it was in Baghban'.
actor_transformation: Not driven by the marriage; his son's death drives his progressive stand.
female_transformation: Shobhna moves from fearing the loss of her grandson to accepting Millie's remarriage.
relationship_outcome: United when the family blesses Millie and Rajat's marriage.
relationship_analysis: The marriage is the first place Balraj's progressive idea is tested. Shobhna's resistance comes from grief and fear of losing Ansh rather than orthodoxy, which makes her objection sympathetic and her change of heart part of the film's argument. The relationship stays secondary to Balraj's bond with Millie, and a modern reading might note that the older couple debate a widow's future largely without her.
critical_reading: Rediff (2006) compared the pairing unfavourably with Baghban, finding it 'not as spontaneous in Baabul'.

initial_relationship: His daughter Ritu's teenage friend, staying with the family for the holidays.
how_they_meet: Ritu brings Jia to spend the holidays at her family's home in Kerala.
who_initiates: Mutual; Jia 'professes some affinity to Vijay' (Wikipedia), and his photographs of her mark the turn.
courtship_pattern: After he photographs her in the garden, 'something innocent grows into something bigger' and then 'beyond control' (Wikipedia); they kiss, and Vijay confesses his love for Jia to his wife.
emotional_dynamic: An introverted older man awakened by a restless, effervescent teenager; Rediff describes 'the inevitable spark, the undeniable chemistry' of an odd couple.
pair_conflict: No conflict between them is described; the obstacles are his family and her age.
pair_friction_explanation: Little conflict between them until Vijay, persuaded of her vulnerability, orders her to leave.
external_opposition_explanation: His marriage, his daughter's discovery and his brother-in-law Shridhar's intervention end the affair.
lover_boy_explanation: Consumed by love for Jia, he confesses it to his wife and lives on in her memory; the role is organised around the romance, as an older man's infatuation rather than a heroic courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Rediff's Raja Sen praised 'the undeniable chemistry, between this perfectly cast odd-couple'.
actor_transformation: The infatuation breaks his marriage and leaves him contemplating suicide.
female_transformation: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_outcome: Vijay sends Jia away and is left estranged from his family, living in her memory.
relationship_analysis: Nishabd frames the relationship from inside Vijay's longing, through his narration from a precipice, the photographs and a languid first half, and Rediff read it as a charged odd-couple romance. The film supplies its own corrective through Shridhar, who makes Vijay see that at Jia's 'vulnerable and naive age' even a small helping gesture can seem like love. A modern reading would stress the power imbalance between a married man and his daughter's teenage friend, which the film acknowledges but also romanticises.
critical_reading: Rediff (2007) praised the 'undeniable chemistry' of the 'perfectly cast odd-couple' in a 'bold, punchy film'; Wikipedia notes that Bachchan denied the film was inspired by Lolita.

The ending, with wife and daughter having lost trust in him, treats the damage to the marriage as Vijay's punishment rather than exploring her response.
critical_reading: Rediff (2007) introduces Amrita (Revathy) only as the wife with whom Vijay lives on the tea estate; no fetched review discusses the marriage.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he humiliates her after she sends back a dish at his restaurant.
how_they_meet: Visiting London, Nina sends back a pulao as too sweet at Buddha's restaurant; he derides her, and she has a better pulao sent to him.
who_initiates: Mutual; after Buddha tries to apologise, 'they slowly fall in love' (Wikipedia).
courtship_pattern: Sarcasm turns to witty repartee on rainy London days, with Nina borrowing the chef's umbrella (Rediff), and they decide to marry despite a 30-year age gap.
emotional_dynamic: Sparring equals: Rediff says Nina 'has spirit', which 'lends the pair contrast, gives it chemistry'.
pair_conflict: They argue constantly over her father's opposition.
pair_friction_explanation: Early hostility, then repeated arguments over her father's hunger strike that leave Buddha heartbroken.
external_opposition_explanation: Nina's father, who is younger than Buddha, goes on a Gandhian hunger strike against the marriage before relenting.
lover_boy_explanation: An unconventional romantic hero: the ageing, sarcastic chef's courtship and heartbreak drive the film.
chemistry_explanation: Rediff wrote that Nina 'lends the pair contrast, gives it chemistry, makes the film work', and that 'the repartee between the lead pair is tight'.
actor_transformation: Love and grief soften the arrogant chef, who ends up bonding with Nina's father over cricket.
female_transformation: Not described in the fetched sources.
relationship_outcome: Together with her father's blessing; both families gather at Buddha's restaurant.
relationship_analysis: Cheeni Kum plays the May–December romance as a comedy of manners: the couple's sparring gives Nina equal footing, and the obstacle is her father's discomfort with a son-in-law older than himself. The film treats the age gap as a prejudice to overcome rather than a power imbalance, a framing that holds because Nina is confident and self-directed. Buddha's grief for his young friend Sexy supplies the emotional turn that reconciles the lovers.
critical_reading: Rediff (2007) called it 'a deftly made May-December love story that ends up being both relatable and romanticised', crediting Nina's spirit for the pair's chemistry.

lover_boy_explanation: Romantic songs with Hema ('romantic ditties', per The Times of India) within an action-comedy role centred on protecting his son.
chemistry_explanation: Sify (quoted by Wikipedia) said 'the Amitabh-Hema portions' create 'magic momentarily', and Nikhat Kazmi noted his 'romantic ditties (with Hema)'.
actor_transformation: His acceptance of his age at the hospital coincides with his reconciliation with Sita.
female_transformation: Sita moves from refusing him to reconciling, while still forbidding him to reveal himself to Karan.
relationship_outcome: Reconciled; Vijju returns to Paris, and Sita will bring Karan to him when she is ready.
relationship_analysis: The marriage carries the film's sentimental subplot: Sita embodies the cost of Vijju's violent past, and her first refusal gives the reconciliation some weight. She keeps control of the family secret, deciding when Karan will learn the truth, which gives her more agency than her brief screen time suggests. The casting repeats the Bachchan–Hema Malini pairing of Baghban and Baabul.
critical_reading: Wikipedia quotes The Times of India's Nikhat Kazmi on his 'romantic ditties (with Hema)' and Sify on 'the Amitabh-Hema portions, where they create magic momentarily'.

initial_relationship: Long-married couple, he a resident son-in-law dependent on her property
how_they_meet: Not shown; the marriage predates the story by decades
courtship_pattern: None depicted
emotional_dynamic: Mercenary cohabitation without affection: he waits out her life, she humours him and finally outwits him
pair_conflict: Mirza wants Fatima Mahal and can only inherit it when Begum dies, so her continued life is the obstacle to his one ambition
pair_friction_explanation: The friction is one-sided but severe and structural: Mirza resents his wife's survival, schemes to have the mansion transferred to himself, and goes as far as stealing her fingerprints while she sleeps so a lawyer can forge her consent. She is not hostile to him in return, which keeps this below the register of open mutual antagonism.
external_opposition_explanation: The pressure on the marriage comes from the property rather than from any person opposing the couple: the tenants' refusal to pay, the government archaeologist's plan to seize the mansion as a heritage site, and the developer's offer all bear on Mirza's calculation rather than on any bond between the two.
lover_boy_explanation: The role is the exact inverse of the lover-boy archetype. Mirza shows no romantic feeling, devotion or sacrifice at any point; the marriage is purely instrumental to him, and the film's comedy depends on the audience recognising that.
actor_transformation: None; he ends as grasping as he began, merely defeated
female_transformation: None required: Begum is revealed to have been in command of her own position throughout
relationship_outcome: Begum disappears, having secretly eloped with her old lover Abdul Rehman and sold Fatima Mahal to him for one rupee to preserve it, leaving Mirza a letter. She returns to the mansion at 95 to celebrate her birthday with her lover while Mirza and Baankey are shut out.
relationship_analysis: The most unsentimental marriage in Bachchan's filmography and the clearest late-career inversion of his romantic persona. Mirza's entire relation to his wife is actuarial: he married into her property and now waits for her to die, and the film measures his moral smallness by how openly he counts the days. The reversal is that Begum has been running her own plan the whole time. Her elopement with a lover she never gave up, and the sale of the mansion for a token rupee, deny Mirza the inheritance and expose that the woman he treated as a delay was the only person in the film with a design worth the name.
critical_reading: Reviewers read the film through the Mirza-Baankey duel rather than the marriage, which is why the ending lands as a surprise; a modern reading notes that the film hands its oldest woman both the sexual autonomy and the property outcome, while the two men who spend the film fighting over her house are left with nothing.
